summary: This document extends the Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF) from RFC 5070 so organizations can exchange richer cybersecurity information. It gives a pattern to embed structured information consistently.

eli5.summary: When security teams share reports about attacks, they need a common form. This adds spaces for detailed, machine-readable facts.

questions: what is the iodef structured cybersecurity information extension
how to embed xml in iodef
what is the iodef sci iana registry
subtitle: A standard way to embed structured vulnerability, attack and remediation data inside IODEF incident reports.

tldr.problem: IODEF can describe an incident, but it has no detailed format for things like attack patterns, vulnerabilities or severity scores, so such details end up as free-form text that machines cannot process.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7203 defines eight extension classes that wrap data written in other specifications, either as embedded XML or as a reference, and an IANA registry of the specifications that may be used.
tldr.outcome: Incident reports can carry machine-readable security data that receivers can store, look up and pass on without human intervention.

today: RFC 7203 is a Proposed Standard, published in April 2014, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the format defined in RFC 5070.

sections.title: Why Extend IODEF
sections.content:
Incident information has to be reported, exchanged and shared between organizations, and the Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF, from RFC 5070) is one tool for that. To run security operations efficiently, the information needs to be machine readable, but IODEF often has to carry unstructured incident data to convey specifics.

Many structured formats for cybersecurity information already exist, among them CAPEC, CCE, CVE, CVSS, CWE, CPE, OVAL and SCAP. Embedding them in IODEF documents lets the receiver get fuller context and automate more of its work. Because IODEF is flexible and extensible, the RFC defines an extension rather than a new report format, and provides only the structures needed for embedding.
sections.eli5: Reports about attacks used to be mostly written notes. This lets teams attach tidy, labelled facts that computers can read on their own.

sections.title: Where This Applies
sections.content:
Organizations need to exchange attack patterns, platform information, vulnerabilities and weaknesses, countermeasure instructions, computer event logs and severity assessments. IODEF can carry these but does not define detailed formats for them. This extension borrows existing formats.

The RFC gives two scenarios. A sender reporting an incident can embed an XML attack pattern record instead of describing the exploit in free text, and the receiver can look up its tags, store it and forward it with no human involved. In another, an administrator who found a configuration problem generates an XML software configuration description, embeds it in an IODEF document and sends it to a partner to prevent the same event there.
sections.eli5: A sender can attach a ready-made fact sheet about the attack. The receiver's computer can read it, file it and share it with friends automatically.

sections.title: The Extension Design and the IANA Table
sections.content:
The extension adds new classes that sit inside the AdditionalData and RecordItem classes of IODEF. One data type is added, XMLDATA, for embedded XML: an extension of iodef:ExtensionType whose dtype is xml.

The supported specifications are listed in an IANA table. Each entry has a namespace, specification name, version, reference URI and the classes it applies to. The initial table has one entry: the Malware Metadata Exchange Format (MMDEF) version 1.2, namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:mile:mmdef:1.2, applicable to the AttackPattern class. Implementations need not support every entry but must at minimum support that one. If a receiver gets data it does not support, it may look up the table or tell the sender it cannot parse the data. Automatic mass download from the IANA site is not recommended.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of fact-sheet types that everyone agrees on. A receiver only has to understand the one on the starter list.

sections.title: The Eight Extension Classes
sections.content:
The eight classes are AttackPattern, Platform, Vulnerability, Scoring, Weakness, EventReport, Verification and Remediation. Where they live in an Incident differs: AttackPattern, Vulnerability and Weakness go in Method.AdditionalData; Platform goes in AttackPattern, Vulnerability, Weakness or System; Scoring goes in Vulnerability or Weakness; EventReport goes in a RecordItem; Verification and Remediation go in Incident.AdditionalData. The RFC RECOMMENDS including them wherever the information is available.

All eight share a basic structure. Three attributes: SpecID (REQUIRED, chosen from the IANA table namespaces or private), ext-SpecID (OPTIONAL, MUST be used only when SpecID is private) and ContentID (OPTIONAL identifier of the information). Two elements: RawData (zero or more complete XML documents) and Reference (zero or more links). One of ContentID, RawData or Reference MUST be used, and only one SHOULD be, to avoid confusing the receiver.

AttackPattern additionally can hold Platform elements, while Vulnerability and Weakness can hold both Platform and Scoring elements.
sections.eli5: All eight slots work the same way: say which fact-sheet type you use, then either attach the sheet, point to it, or give its ID number.

sections.title: Mandatory-to-Implement Features
sections.content:
A compliant implementation MUST be able to send and receive extended IODEF documents that contain XML conforming to the specification in the initial IANA table (MMDEF 1.2) without error. The extended document MUST be well-formed XML and valid against the schemata available to the validator, including extension schemata.

The RFC includes an example IODEF document carrying MMDEF metadata inside an AttackPattern, generated with the genMMDEF tool from EICAR test files, so implementers can check conformance. It also includes an XML schema for the extension, with a BasicStructure type shared by the classes.
sections.eli5: To be allowed to play, a program must be able to read the starter fact sheet, and the RFC includes a sample so it can practise.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The format is only a data representation and does not directly introduce security issues, but parties exchanging it will have concerns. The messaging and transport used MUST ensure appropriate confidentiality, integrity and authenticity. The RFC points to RFC 6545 (RID) and RFC 6546 (RID over HTTP/TLS) for detailed requirements.

IODEF has a restriction attribute that marks sensitivity, and its use at the application level is RECOMMENDED. XML digital signatures and encryption can protect reports where transmission security is questionable. The critical concerns are that structured information may be falsified, accessed by unintended parties, or corrupted in transit.

Incident data is often sensitive and may contain private information about people or organizations. The RFC RECOMMENDS establishing policies and procedures for exchange beforehand, since these often need legal review and executive approval, and that systems storing or exchanging the data be secured, run minimal services and keep access controls and monitoring.
sections.eli5: Attack reports can contain secrets, so they should travel in locked envelopes, and teams should agree on the sharing rules before they start.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:iodef-sci-1.0 and the XML schema urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:iodef-sci-1.0. It also created the registry "Structured Cybersecurity Information (SCI) Specifications" under the IODEF registry, holding the namespace, specification name, version, reference URI and applicable classes. A registered specification MUST be publicly available at its URI and MUST only be used with the classes in its entry.

The allocation policy is Specification Required, which includes Expert Review. The Designated Expert is expected to consult the MILE (Managed Incident Lightweight Exchange) working group, check that the specification is reachable and check that the listed classes are appropriate.
sections.eli5: IANA keeps the official list of fact-sheet types, and an expert checks any newcomer before it is added.

items.title: AttackPattern
items.text: Attack patterns of incidents, in Method.AdditionalData.

items.title: Vulnerability
items.text: Vulnerabilities exposed or exploited, in Method.AdditionalData.

items.title: Weakness
items.text: Weakness types exposed or exploited, in Method.AdditionalData.

items.title: Scoring
items.text: Severity scores for a vulnerability or weakness.

items.title: EventReport
items.text: Structured event reports, in a RecordItem.

items.title: Verification
items.text: Security verification such as a checklist.
